edition: Issue 053: New Zealand counts to 2pm and hopes for a Government, the Barretts hand the captaincy around like a family heirloom, and a Christchurch queen does pageant spins on a broken toe
tagline: Your 3-minute Friday reset: a final vote count so tight 139 people decide the Government, a third Barrett becomes All Blacks captain after a record hiding, and a top-5 Miss Universe run built on a gym plate and zero chill.

stories.headline: Deal or deadlock: the final election count lands at 2pm, and about 400,000 special votes could decide who governs
stories.summary: The Electoral Commission publishes the official 2026 election result at 2pm today, adding roughly 400,000 special votes that could keep the National-led coalition, deadlock Parliament, or turn Opportunity into kingmaker - after three weeks that have left Christopher Luxon bewildered.

body.text: The three-week wait for the official count ends at 2pm today, when the Electoral Commission publishes the final result of the 2026 general election. Election night gave the National, ACT and New Zealand First coalition 67 of a swollen 131-seat Parliament - just one past the 66 needed to govern - while Labour, the Greens and Te Pati Maori held 57 and the Opportunity Party seven. Now roughly 400,000 special votes - cast from overseas, away from home or not on the printed roll - get added to the tallies, in an election so close that on the preliminary count Labour (29.36%) beat National (29.21%) in the party vote by just 3,650 votes. The closest electorate, Wairarapa, is split by 139 votes. The result could return the coalition, force a deadlock, or hand the balance of power to the Opportunity Party leadership. RNZ runs through three ways it could land, and notes recounts are all but certain, with candidates given three working days to apply.

Nothing says mature democracy quite like three weeks of politicking ending in a situation where the entire direction of the country could turn on 139 people in one electorate - and a recount you have to literally pay NZ$92,000 for the privilege of requesting. We have built a political system where a bewildered Christopher Luxon and a conspicuously quiet Chris Hipkins have spent a fortnight staring at spreadsheets produced by a medley of mathematicians, with varying levels of proficiency. The modelling says it could go any of three ways; the only honest forecaster in the country has concluded the sensible move is to just wait until 2pm. You suspect the nation would get roughly the same reliability from three of us in an office car park, except we would charge a lot less to recount, and we would do it for sausage rolls.

RNZ (27 Nov 2026, Craig McCulloch, Deal or deadlock: Three ways today's final count could land) and Stuff (26 Nov 2026, Jenna Lynch and Emma Ricketts, What to watch out for in the special votes): the Electoral Commission publishes the official election result at 2pm on Friday 27 November, adding an estimated 400,000 special votes to the roughly 2.4 million ordinary votes counted on election night. Preliminary results: National 42, Labour 36, Greens 16, ACT 13, NZ First 12, Opportunity 7, Te Pati Maori 5 (131 seats, 11 overhang; 66 needed to govern); party vote Labour 29.36%/710,330 vs National 29.21%/706,680 (a 3,650-vote margin). Wairarapa is the closest electorate (National's Mike Butterick leads Labour's Kieran McAnulty by 139 votes). RNZ's three scenarios: the coalition holds or strengthens; a 65-65 deadlock where Opportunity could back the right bloc on confidence-and-supply; or Opportunity as kingmaker able to anoint a National- or Labour-led government. Candidates have three working days to request recounts; a nationwide party-vote recount requires a NZ$92,000 deposit (RNZ notes Waitakere flipped on a recount in 2011).

stories.headline: Jordie Barrett to captain the All Blacks for the first time - the third Barrett brother to wear the armband - with six changes for the England rematch
stories.summary: Dave Rennie names Jordie Barrett captain for the All Blacks' Nations Championship rematch against England at Twickenham, making him the third Barrett brother to lead the side after a record 37-12 defeat last weekend, with six starting changes including Richie Mo'unga at fly-half.

body.text: Jordie Barrett will captain the All Blacks for the first time in Sunday's (NZT) Nations Championship rematch against England at Twickenham, stepping in after tour captain Codie Taylor was ruled out with a calf injury. The announcement makes Jordie the third Barrett brother to lead New Zealand, after Scott and Beauden - Beauden captained the side two weeks ago in the shock loss to Wales in Cardiff. It comes on the back of the All Blacks' record 37-12 defeat to England at the same venue last weekend, which left the team facing the prospect of their worst professional-era season. Rennie has made six starting changes, four injury-enforced, with Will Jordan, Tupou Vaa'i and Anton Lienert-Brown joining Taylor on the sidelines. Richie Mo'unga comes in at first-five, Damian McKenzie shifts to fullback, Rieko Ioane returns on the wing, and Beauden Barrett drops to the bench. 'Huge congratulations to Jordie on being named captain,' Rennie said. 'He's been a key part of our leadership group for a long time and is highly respected by his team-mates, on and off-field.'

Some families keep their grandmother's china as an heirloom; the Barretts just keep trading the All Blacks captaincy between brothers. Scott has led it, Beauden has led it, and now the youngest is getting a turn - which is one way of handling a record 37-12 hiding: if at first you don't succeed, keep trying a Barrett. Dave Rennie has, to be fair, found the single most wholesome available response to sporting catastrophe: put the armband on the guy who never looked like switching off even when the rest of the team was on holiday. And if you need a little extra sibling chaos to enjoy it, note that the brother he will lead this weekend is on the bench, after last week's news the oldest reportedly has his eye on Bristol. There is nothing NZ rugby cannot be sorted out by a family barbecue. Kick it over to Jordie, lads - and this time do it on purpose.

NZ Herald (27 Nov 2026, All Blacks v England: Jordie Barrett to captain amid surprise selections for rematch), Stuff (27 Nov 2026, Jordie Barrett to captain All Blacks as Dave Rennie makes six changes) and RNZ (27 Nov 2026, Six changes to All Blacks team as they seek redemption against England): Jordie Barrett captains the All Blacks for the first time in the Nations Championship rematch against England at Twickenham on Sunday (NZT), after tour captain Codie Taylor was ruled out with a calf injury; he becomes the third Barrett brother to captain the side, after Scott and Beauden (Beauden led in the loss to Wales in Cardiff two weeks ago). The side were beaten 37-12 by England at the same venue the previous weekend, a record professional-era defeat. Rennie made six starting changes, four injury-enforced (Taylor, Will Jordan, Tupou Vaa'i and Anton Lienert-Brown out); Richie Mo'unga starts at first-five, Damian McKenzie moves to fullback, Rieko Ioane returns on the wing, and Beauden Barrett is on the bench. Rennie: 'Huge congratulations to Jordie on being named captain... a massively proud moment for him and the Barrett whanau.'

stories.headline: A broken toe, a 10kg gym plate and a tiara: Christchurch's Georgia Waddington takes a top-5 Miss Universe finish - New Zealand's best in 43 years
stories.summary: 25-year-old Christchurch beauty queen and entrepreneur Georgia Waddington placed top 5 at the 75th Miss Universe in Puerto Rico - New Zealand's highest Miss Universe ranking in 43 years - after dropping a gym plate on her toe four weeks out, being told to avoid heels for six weeks, and putting them back on after two.

body.text: Georgia Waddington from Christchurch has made history as the first New Zealander in 43 years to reach the top 5 at Miss Universe, placing fifth at the 75th pageant in Puerto Rico. The 25-year-old beauty queen and entrepreneur, who competed against 115 others, did it with an injury she refused to let stop her. Four weeks out from the contest she broke her toe at the gym, dropping a roughly 10kg plate on it from hip height. She was told to stay out of heels for six weeks; she put her heels back on after two and trained through the pain, because, as she told RNZ's Afternoons, 'I couldn't back out now.' Her national costume, designed to evoke the Pink and White Terraces destroyed by the 1886 Mt Tarawera eruption, was apparently her mum's idea. The highest-ranked New Zealander before her was Lisa Maree de Montalk, who reached the top 10 in 1992; Lorraine Downes won the title outright in 1983.

The classic pre-grand-final checklist for a beauty queen: rehearsals, interviews, eight judges with roughly three minutes each to sell your whole life, a costume themed on a volcano that erupted in the 1800s - and, if you are Georgia Waddington, a 10kg plate landing on your toe a month out and being politely advised by doctors to keep off the heels for six weeks. She put them back on in two. That is not determination so much as it is refusing to let a small toe injury get between you and the moment you have been rehearsing since you were a girl clicking around the house in plastic heels and a tiara. It is an entirely wholesome kind of chaos, and it got New Zealand its best Miss Universe result in 43 years. Someone please give that toe - and that mum with the terrace costume idea - a medal. Actually, give them the ones in the top five.

RNZ (25 Nov 2026, Afternoons, Georgia Waddington's broken-toe road to Miss Universe top 5): Georgia Waddington, 25, from Christchurch, placed in the top 5 at the 75th Miss Universe contest in Puerto Rico - the first New Zealander to do so in 43 years. Four weeks before the final she broke her toe at the gym after dropping a roughly 10kg plate on it from hip height; advised to stay out of heels for six weeks, she returned to heels after two weeks and continued training. She competed against 115 others. In the national costume round she wore an outfit evoking the Pink and White Terraces, destroyed in the 1886 Mt Tarawera eruption - an idea she attributed to her mother. The last New Zealander to rank as highly was Lisa Maree de Montalk (top 10 in 1992); Lorraine Downes won the title in 1983.
